extracted.intended_audience: readers of social/political philosophy and higher-education critics (college educators, intellectuals, general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic theory explaining the law of human progress: that 'association in equality' drives civilization forward and that external (geographic) and internal (inequality, habit, institutional inertia) resistances check or reverse progress. Also includes a related meditation on the social role and aims of colleges in shaping democratic 'tone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Colleges should cultivate a liberal outlook and perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: If colleges are 'the yeast cake for democracy's dough' they must show every subject in its place within the 'whole policy of mankind' and provide a liberal outlook that surrounds subjects with perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colleges should let in every modern subject, keep settings wide enough so any subject becomes humanistic, and show students how technical bargains fit into broader human concerns (e.g., a technical school enables a bargain splendidly, but a college should show its place in mankind's policy). This is an educative aim for shaping democratic preferences and civic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colleges must spread a healthy, sympathetic 'tone' rather than exclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: "Tone" is the vague but central quality by which institutions either lose or save human things; colleges must adopt a hearty, sympathetic tone that resists priggishness and exclusiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real culture 'lives by sympathies and admirations, not by dislikes and disdains.' Colleges make students immune to snobbishness by maintaining a general tone that is 'too hearty for the microbe's life.' Teachers' tone has high spreading power via imitation; colleges should aim for the tone most capable of influencing democracy positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colleges' primary practical aim: enabling the recognition of 'better men'
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal result colleges ought to aim for is enabling people to 'know a good man when you see him'—i.e., to indicate the better men to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although diffuse, this synthetic formula (knowing a good man when you see him) should guide faculties and graduates as the underlying purpose that clarifies many problems and increases institutional influence in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association in equality is the fundamental law of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: "Association in equality" — the combination of social cooperation (association) and justice/equality — is identified as the law under which civilization advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Association frees mental power for improvement (division of labor, co-operation), while equality (justice) prevents wasted effort in conflict and the dissipation of mental power. Together they explain diverse historical patterns of rise, halt, and retrogression of civilizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental power as the motor of progress; its allocation matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental power (the faculty to extend knowledge and skill) is the motor of progress but is finite; progress depends on how much mental power is devoted to improvement rather than maintenance or conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-progressive uses of mental power are classified as maintenance (support of existence and preserving social arrangements) and conflict (warfare, aggression, seeking gains at others' expense). Reducing maintenance/conflict increases mental power available for progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: External resistances (geography, climate, resources) determine ease of early association
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical conditions — climate, soil, terrain — affect how closely people can associate, thus affecting where and how early civilization arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rich plains and favorable climates allow closer association, lower subsistence costs, and more mental power for improvement; harsh or isolating environments limit association and slow development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms that promote association (commerce, conquest, religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce, certain forms of conquest (that create larger peaceful units), and sometimes religion operate to extend association and thereby advance civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commerce builds interdependence and interests opposed to warfare; conquest that unites smaller communities can secure internal peace and foster association; religion has at times mitigated war and promoted union (e.g., Christianity's role in Europe's development). Each mechanism has contextual effects that can either help or harm progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal resistances (inequality, habit, institutional inertia) produce petrifaction
rubrics_metrics.description: As societies integrate and specialize, there is a constant tendency toward inequality; this unequal distribution of wealth and power wastes mental power and leads to petrifaction or retrogression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two human qualities—power of habit and possibility of mental/moral deterioration—cause social adjustments (laws, customs, institutions) to persist beyond usefulness. Concentrated power and privilege entrench conservatism, resist innovation, and turn knowledge into secret or privilege-maintaining reserves rather than common improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and integration often generate class concentration of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The specialization of functions (military, religious, administrative) naturally tends to lodge collective power in particular classes (military chiefs, priests), which then magnify their function and extend their power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While specialization increases productive power, it also creates vested interests whose growth fosters inequality; selection of leaders becomes more difficult in large societies, encouraging blind obedience and absolute power unless checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private ownership and natural monopoly of land is a primary source of inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriation of land and the arising of rent, together with the concentration of land ownership in ruling classes, is the great cause of inequality that dries up the strength of civilizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial notions of common land devolve into private ownership as population grows; as rent appears, ownership concentrates via conquest and political power, converting masses into tenants and reducing the capacity for broader social improvement. Public appropriation of rent for common purposes is presented as the only way to retain land as common property at advanced stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality reshapes inventive effort toward luxury and ostentation rather than public improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When inequality predominates, the inventive energies of society are diverted to refinements of luxury and ostentation rather than to innovations that relieve toil and increase common power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge becomes hidden or suppressed if it threatens privileged orders; the masses' mental power is expended in maintenance of existence rather than improvement, and elites resist innovations that would erode their advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small, steady cultural forces accumulate more than large intermittent ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A small force, if continuous, will produce cumulative effects more considerable than larger forces acting inconsistently; the steady whisper of permanent ideals (truth and justice) will, given time, warp the world in their direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle supports the importance of continuous cultural influence (e.g., colleges, intellectuals) in shaping democratic tone and long-term social improvement rather than relying on sporadic major movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: If higher institutions fail to influence public opinion, other popular media will supplant them
rubrics_metrics.description: Colleges must maintain influence over public taste and opinion; if they lose it, popular periodicals and 'ten-cent magazines' may become the de facto educators of the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage names popular magazines (McClure's, American Magazine, Collier's Weekly, World's Work) as an emergent 'popular university'—a warning that failure by colleges to spread culture broadly will cede cultural leadership to mass-market media.
